etymology: From Latin natio, “birth, people,” rendering Hebrew goy and Greek ethnos, a people bound by common descent, tongue, and bound habitation.
biblical_def: Nationhood is the divine ordering of the human race into distinct peoples, made of one blood, set within appointed bounds, and gathered at last from every nation around the throne of the Lamb. Paul declares at Athens that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26). The nations themselves are no accident of history but the work of the LORD, who at Babel scattered the families of the sons of Noah, “every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations” (Gen 10:32), and who “set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel” (Deu 32:8). Thus the existence of nations, with their borders, languages, and peoples, is a providential good, ordained for the dwelling and ordering of fallen men. Yet nationhood is never an ultimate. It serves a higher end, for the gospel goes out to all nations, and the redeemed are gathered as “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9). Every nation stands under the Lord Jesus Christ, who is King of kings; and the diversity of the peoples is not erased but redeemed, brought to bow before one Saviour and to praise one God.
webster_summary: The divine ordering of mankind into distinct peoples, made of one blood within appointed bounds, gathered at last from every nation to Christ.
webster_full: NATIONHOOD, the divinely ordained ordering of mankind into distinct peoples.

The LORD set the bounds of the people in His providence (Deu 32:8).
The redeemed are gathered from all nations before the throne (Rev 7:9).

corruption_summary: Two errors assail biblical nationhood: the globalist erasure of nations, and the idolatrous ethno-nationalism that makes blood and soil an ultimate; Christ alone is Lord over all nations.
corruption_paragraphs: On the one hand stands the globalist erasure of nations, which treats borders, peoples, and tongues as relics to be dissolved into a single undifferentiated mass of humanity. This denies the work of God, who Himself divided the nations after Babel and set the bounds of their habitation. The diversity of the peoples is His ordering, not a problem to be abolished; to seek the melting of all nations into one earthly empire is to repeat the very sin of Babel, which the LORD came down to scatter.

On the other hand stands an idolatrous ethno-nationalism, which exalts blood and soil into an ultimate and makes a man’s people, rather than the Lord Jesus Christ, the object of his highest loyalty. This too is a corruption, for it forgets that God made of one blood all nations, that every nation stands under judgment, and that the redeemed are gathered from every kindred and tongue. The Christian loves his own people rightly, as a gift of providence, but he worships only Christ, before whom every nation must bow. Nationhood is a good servant and a damnable god; it must be kept under the lordship of the King of kings.
roots_summary: From Latin natio, “a people,” rendering the Hebrew goy and Greek ethnos, the divinely bounded peoples of the earth.

etymology: From the Lord’s own words to Pilate, “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36), naming the spiritual nature and heavenly origin of Christ’s reign.
biblical_def: The kingdom of Christ is a real and present reign, but it is “not of this world” (Joh 18:36) — not earthly in its origin, its weapons, or its character. When Pilate asked whether He were a king, the Lord answered that His kingdom was not of this world, else would His servants fight; its source is heaven, and its advance is not by sword or vote but by the Word and the Spirit. So too the Lord taught that “the kingdom of God cometh not with observation: neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you” (Luk 17:20–21), reigning first in the hearts of His people. Paul defines its substance: “the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost” (Rom 14:17). This kingdom is entered by the new birth, for the Father “hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son” (Col 1:13). It is not anti-worldly in the sense of fleeing all earthly duty, for Christ is Lord of all spheres; but its nature is spiritual, its citizens are the regenerate, and its consummation awaits His bodily return. The Church does not build the kingdom by political conquest; she proclaims the King, who reigns now at the Father’s right hand and will reign visibly when He comes again.
webster_summary: The spiritual, heavenly reign of Christ, not earthly in origin or weapon, advanced by Word and Spirit, consummated at His return.
webster_full: KINGDOM NOT OF THIS WORLD, the spiritual and heavenly reign of Christ.

It is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost (Rom 14:17).

corruption_summary: The kingdom is corrupted whenever it is collapsed into earthly politics — by the political-messianism of left and right, and by liberation theology that makes the gospel a programme of revolution.
corruption_paragraphs: A corruption arises wherever the kingdom is collapsed into earthly politics, as if Christ came to seize a throne in this age by the arm of flesh. Political-messianism on the right, which would baptize a nation or a ruler as the engine of the kingdom, and political-messianism on the left, which would make the kingdom a programme of social reconstruction, both forget the Lord’s word to Pilate. His kingdom is not of this world; it does not come by the sword or the ballot, and no party or state is its bearer. To pin the hope of Christ’s reign to a candidate or a revolution is to seek a Christ Pilate could understand — an earthly king — and to miss the King who reigns from heaven.

Liberation theology, named explicitly, is the gravest form of this error: a progressive framework, born of Gutiérrez and his heirs, that fuses the gospel with Marxist categories and collapses salvation into the political liberation of the oppressed in this present age. It reads the exodus and the kingdom as a manifesto of earthly revolution and makes the Church an arm of class struggle. Scripture rebukes it plainly. The kingdom of God is “righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost” (Rom 14:17), entered by the new birth, not by the overthrow of an economic order. Christ delivers men from the power of darkness, not merely from earthly want; and to reduce His everlasting kingdom to a temporal struggle is to lose the gospel itself.
roots_summary: From the Lord’s testimony before Pilate, declaring the heavenly origin and spiritual nature of His reign.

usage: Do not pin the hope of Christ’s reign to a party, a ruler, or a revolution; His kingdom is not of this world.
Reject liberation theology, which collapses the everlasting kingdom into earthly class struggle.
Seek first the kingdom that is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost, entered by the new birth.

etymology: The relation of national Israel and the New Testament Church, figured by Paul as one olive tree (Rom 11:17), the “Israel of God” (Gal 6:16).
biblical_def: The Scripture knows but one people of God in all ages, one olive tree into which both Jew and Gentile are grafted by faith. Paul teaches that the Gentile believer is “graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree” (Rom 11:17), while unbelieving branches are broken off and may be grafted in again if they abide not in unbelief (Rom 11:23–24). There is no second tree; there is the one cultivated olive, Israel, into which the wild branches of the nations are brought. Thus the Church is not a parenthesis nor a separate people, but the continuation and fullness of the covenant people, and Paul blesses “the Israel of God” (Gal 6:16) upon all who walk by the new creation. He insists that “they are not all Israel, which are of Israel” (Rom 9:6), for the true seed is the children of the promise, not merely of the flesh (Rom 9:7–8). In Christ the dividing wall is broken down, for He hath “made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14), making of Jew and Gentile “one new man” (Eph 2:15). There remains a glorious hope for ethnic Israel, a remnant according to the election of grace and a fullness yet to come; but their salvation is by grafting into the one tree, not by a separate way. One Saviour, one covenant of grace, one people of God.
webster_summary: The one olive tree of God’s people, into which Jew and Gentile are grafted by faith; the Church is the fullness of the covenant people, not a separate body.
webster_full: ISRAEL AND THE CHURCH, the one people of God in all ages.

corruption_summary: Dispensationalism corrupts the doctrine by dividing God’s people into two permanently distinct peoples, Israel and the Church, on two separate tracks — a nineteenth-century novelty unknown to the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The gravest corruption of this doctrine is the dispensational two-peoples theology, which permanently divides Israel and the Church into two distinct peoples of God with two distinct destinies, two programmes, and (in its older forms) even two ways of relating to God. On this scheme the Church is a parenthesis, an interruption in God’s dealings with national Israel, to be set aside at the rapture so that the earthly programme may resume. But Paul knows only one olive tree, not two; he grafts the Gentiles into Israel, not alongside her. To make two permanent peoples is to saw the one tree in half and to deny that Christ has made of the two “one new man.”

This division is a nineteenth-century novelty, not the faith of the Church. It was systematized by John Nelson Darby and popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible; it appears in no Reformation confession, in no Puritan divine, in none of the ancient creeds. The whole Church before Darby read Romans 11 as one tree and the people of God as one. The dictionary therefore rejects the two-peoples scheme as a recent innovation that fractures the unity of the covenant of grace. There is one Saviour, one covenant, one people — with a real and glorious hope yet remaining for ethnic Israel, who shall be saved by being grafted again into their own olive tree.

etymology: From Latin occultus, “hidden, secret,” naming the forbidden arts of divination, witchcraft, and traffic with spirits that God’s law condemns.
biblical_def: The occult is the whole body of forbidden arts by which men seek hidden knowledge or power apart from God — divination, witchcraft, enchantment, the consulting of familiar spirits, and the calling up of the dead. God’s law condemns it root and branch. “There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer. For all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD” (Deu 18:10–12). The same law forbids the very inclination toward such things: “Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God” (Lev 19:31). These are not harmless curiosities but defilements, an abomination, and a turning from the living God to the powers of darkness. When the gospel came to Ephesus, the converts burned their costly books of curious arts before all men (Act 19:19), counting the loss as nothing against Christ. Paul ranks “witchcraft” among the works of the flesh that shut men out of the kingdom of God (Gal 5:19–21). The occult is thus no neutral path to wisdom but a rebellion against the Lord, who alone reveals what He will and forbids His people to seek the hidden things by any door but His Word.
webster_summary: The forbidden arts of divination, witchcraft, and traffic with spirits, condemned by God’s law as an abomination and a turning to the powers of darkness.
webster_full: THE OCCULT, the forbidden arts of hidden knowledge and power apart from God.

corruption_summary: The modern revival of witchcraft, astrology, and spiritism — even creeping into the church — defies God’s law, which names these arts an abomination.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the modern revival of the very arts God’s law condemns: witchcraft repackaged as “wicca” and self-empowerment, astrology and horoscopes consulted as harmless amusement, mediums and spiritism dressed up as comfort for the bereaved, tarot and crystals and enchantments sold as spirituality. The age calls these things a path to wisdom or wellness; God calls them an abomination. There is no neutral ground here. To seek the hidden things by divination is to turn from the living God who reveals Himself in His Word to the powers of darkness who deceive.

Most grievous is the creeping of these practices into the visible church, where some now blend astrology, “manifesting,” the enneagram’s occult roots, contemplative emptying, and Christianized witchcraft with the name of Christ. This is the syncretism the prophets denounced — the worship of the LORD mingled with the rites of the nations. The Ephesian converts knew better; they burned their books of curious arts at great cost when the light of Christ shone. The church today must do the same, renouncing every occult art, however fashionable, and seeking the hidden things only at the door God has opened, His sufficient and finished Word.

etymology: From Latin ager, “field, land,” naming the dignity of tilling and keeping the ground under the dominion God gave to man.
biblical_def: Agrarianism, biblically understood, is the honouring of the dignity of working the ground — the tilling and keeping of the earth under the dominion and stewardship God gave to man at creation. The LORD God “took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it” (Gen 2:15), so that honest labour upon the land was man’s calling before ever sin entered. The land itself was given a holy rhythm under God’s law: six years the field was sown and the vineyard pruned, but the seventh year was “a sabbath of rest unto the land, a sabbath for the LORD” (Lev 25:3–5), that the ground might rest and the poor and the beast might eat. The Psalmist sings of the LORD who “causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man: that he may bring forth food out of the earth” (Psa 104:14), teaching that every harvest is a gift of God’s providence and not the bare product of human toil. And the Preacher observes that “the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field” (Ecc 5:9), so that the labour of the husbandman undergirds the whole commonwealth. Thus Scripture dignifies the plough and the vineyard, commends honest labour and contentment with God’s provision, and binds the keeping of the land to the worship and rest of the LORD.
webster_summary: The honouring of honest labour upon the land, the keeping of the ground under God-given dominion, and the sabbath rest of the field as His providence.
webster_full: AGRARIANISM, the honouring of honest labour and stewardship upon the land.
God put man in the garden to dress it and to keep it (Gen 2:15).
The land was given a sabbath rest in the seventh year (Lev 25:3–5).
The LORD brings forth food out of the earth by His providence (Psa 104:14).
The profit of the earth is for all; the king is served by the field (Ecc 5:9).

corruption_summary: A creational good, not a contested doctrine; it commends stewardship of the land — but pantheist earth-worship that adores the creation rather than the Creator must be gently refused.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the creational dignity of labour upon the land. God put man in the garden to dress it and to keep it before the fall, and after the fall He bound the keeping of the land to the rhythm of sabbath rest. The husbandman’s toil is honourable; the harvest is God’s providence, not man’s achievement; and the profit of the earth is a gift for all. Against the contempt for honest manual labour, and against the modern divorce of men from the soil and the seasons, Scripture commends contentment, stewardship, and gratitude for daily bread out of the ground.

Yet a gentle warning belongs here, lest a right love of the land slide into a wrong worship of it. The modern age is prone to a pantheist earth-religion that adores creation itself — “mother earth,” the cult of nature, a green spirituality that makes the soil sacred in itself. Scripture forbids this plainly, naming those who “worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever” (Rom 1:25). The land is to be kept and stewarded, not deified. The Christian husbandman tills the ground as God’s gift and gives thanks to the Giver; he never bows to the gift in the place of the Lord who made it.

etymology: The biblical name for kidnapping and slave-trading, rendering the Greek andrapodistes, “a stealer of men,” a capital crime under God’s law.
biblical_def: Manstealing is the stealing of a human being — kidnapping a man to sell or to hold him as a slave — and God’s law names it a capital crime. “He that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death” (Exo 21:16). The Deuteronomic law repeats the sentence: “If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him; then that thief shall die” (Deu 24:7). This is the Bible’s own word against the slave trade, for the man-stealer is the kidnapper, the trafficker, the dealer who makes merchandise of persons made in the image of God. The New Testament carries the condemnation forward. Paul ranks “menstealers” among the lawless and disobedient, the ungodly and profane, the murderers and the whoremongers, against whom the law was made (1Ti 1:9–10). And in the lament over fallen Babylon, the Apostle John lists among her unholy merchandise the bodies and “souls of men” (Rev 18:13), so that the trafficking of human beings stands among the sins for which the great city is judged. The whole testimony of Scripture is plain: to seize, sell, or own a man as stolen merchandise is a grievous crime against God and against the image-bearer He made.
webster_summary: The biblical crime of kidnapping and slave-trading — making merchandise of a man — condemned by God’s law as worthy of death.
webster_full: MANSTEALING, the kidnapping or selling of a human being as merchandise.

corruption_summary: Scripture’s own word against the slave trade; the principle to recover is the dignity of every man made in God’s image against the trafficking that makes merchandise of him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God’s law itself condemns the stealing and selling of human beings. Long before any modern movement, the Scripture named manstealing a capital crime and ranked the menstealer among murderers and the profane. The Bible thus furnishes the surest ground against the slave trade and against all trafficking of persons: not the shifting sentiment of the age, but the fixed word of the Lawgiver, who made man in His own image and forbids that he be seized, sold, or held as stolen merchandise.

The corruption to be opposed in our own day is the trafficking of human beings made in God’s image — the buying and selling of men, women, and children for labour or for lust, a trade that flourishes still in the shadows of the modern world. Babylon’s merchandise includes the “souls of men,” and the city is judged for it. The Church must call this sin by its biblical name, manstealing, and answer it with the dignity Scripture confers on every image-bearer. Where the world counts persons as commodities, the people of God confess that no man may be made merchandise, for every soul belongs first to the God who made him.

word: The Jewish Roots of the Faith
pronunciation: the JOO-ish roots of the FAITH
etymology: The acknowledgment that “salvation is of the Jews” (Joh 4:22) and that the gospel came “to the Jew first” (Rom 1:16), Israel being the root of the covenant.
biblical_def: The Christian faith is rooted in the covenant God made with Israel, for the Saviour Himself declared, “ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews” (Joh 4:22). Christ was born of Israel after the flesh, the Scriptures of Israel are the oracles of God, and the gospel went out “to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom 1:16). To Israel, Paul says, “pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever” (Rom 9:4–5). The Church does not stand over against Israel as a stranger, but is grafted into Israel’s own olive tree and inherits Israel’s promises in Christ. Moreover God has not cast away His people whom He foreknew; Paul, “an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom 11:1), stands as the proof, with a remnant according to the election of grace. The honouring of these roots means love for the Jewish people, gratitude for the covenant heritage, and the proclamation of Christ to the Jew first. Yet the root bears the branches, and the branches do not bear the root: it is Christ, the seed of Abraham, in whom the whole tree lives.
webster_summary: The acknowledgment that salvation is of the Jews and the gospel came to the Jew first; the Church is grafted into Israel’s own covenant root in Christ.
webster_full: THE JEWISH ROOTS OF THE FAITH, the covenant heritage of Israel into which the Church is grafted.
The Lord declared that salvation is of the Jews (Joh 4:22).
The gospel went to the Jew first, and also to the Greek (Rom 1:16).
To Israel pertain the covenants, the law, and the fathers (Rom 9:4–5).
God hath not cast away His people; Paul is the proof (Rom 11:1).

corruption_summary: Two errors must be rebutted: replacement-driven anti-Semitism that despises the Jewish people, and Hebrew-roots legalism that puts believers back under the ceremonial law Christ has fulfilled.
corruption_paragraphs: On one side stands the ancient sin of anti-Semitism, often driven by a hard replacement theology that holds God to have utterly cast off the Jewish people and the Church to have simply displaced them. Scripture rebukes this plainly: “Hath God cast away his people? God forbid” (Rom 11:1). The Gentile branch is warned not to boast against the natural branches, for it is the root that bears the branch, not the branch the root. To despise the people of whom Christ came after the flesh, or to imagine that the covenant promises are now spite against Israel rather than fulfilled for her in Christ, is arrogance the Apostle expressly forbids. The remnant of Israel is beloved for the fathers’ sakes, and a fullness is yet to come.

On the other side stands Hebrew-roots legalism, which rightly honours the Jewish soil of the faith but wrongly drags believers back under the ceremonial law — binding Gentile Christians to feast days, dietary rules, sabbaths, and the old shadows as though Christ had not fulfilled them. Paul answers it directly: “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:16–17). The ceremonies were the shadow; Christ is the substance. To return to the shadow once the body has come is to turn from the fulfillment to the figure. Honour the roots; do not return to the husks the Saviour has filled and laid aside.
roots_summary: The covenant heritage of Israel, into which the Church is grafted, with Christ the seed of Abraham as the living root.
roots_lines: The Jewish roots of the faith — Israel is the covenant root.
Salvation is of the Jews (Joh 4:22).
The gospel came to the Jew first (Rom 1:16).
To Israel pertain the covenants and the promises (Rom 9:4).
The root bears the branches; Christ is that root.
usage: Honour the Jewish people and the covenant heritage; reject anti-Semitism, for God hath not cast away His people.
Reject Hebrew-roots legalism that binds believers to the ceremonial law Christ has fulfilled (Col 2:16–17).
Remember the root bears the branches: love Israel, but find the whole tree’s life in Christ alone.

etymology: Hebrew yirath YHWH, the reverent awe and holy dread of God that is “the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10).
biblical_def: The fear of the LORD is the reverent awe, the holy dread, and the worshipful submission that the creature owes to his Maker and Redeemer, and it is the very root and beginning of all true wisdom and knowledge. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding” (Pro 9:10); and again, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction” (Pro 1:7). This fear is no slavish terror that drives the soul from God, but neither is it a mere reverence drained of all dread; it is the trembling adoration of a holy God by a creature who knows his sin and his smallness, joined with love and trust in the same God who is gracious. The Preacher gathers up the whole duty of man in it: “Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man” (Ecc 12:13). Our Lord Himself commands this fear in its highest reach, teaching that we are not to fear man, “but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell” (Mat 10:28). Thus the fear of the LORD holds together the holiness and the goodness of God: He is to be approached with reverence and godly fear, for He is a consuming fire; yet He is the God who draws near in Christ to be loved. To lose this fear is to lose wisdom at its root.
webster_summary: The reverent awe and holy dread of God owed by the creature, the beginning of wisdom and the whole duty of man.
webster_full: THE FEAR OF THE LORD, the reverent awe and holy dread owed to God.
It is the beginning of wisdom and understanding (Pro 9:10).
It is the beginning of knowledge, despised only by fools (Pro 1:7).
To fear God and keep His commandments is the whole duty of man (Ecc 12:13).
We are to fear Him who can destroy both soul and body in hell (Mat 10:28).
scriptures: Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Pro 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
corruption_summary: The therapeutic deity of the age strips God of holiness, presenting a God only of comfort and never of awe — a corruption that loses wisdom at its root.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption of the present age is the therapeutic deity — a God refashioned in the image of a counsellor, all comfort and affirmation, stripped of holiness, justice, and the dread that Scripture everywhere ascribes to Him. This god never warns, never judges, never demands; he exists to soothe, to validate the self, and to make the worshipper feel well. But the God of Scripture is “able to destroy both soul and body in hell” (Mat 10:28), a consuming fire before whom the seraphim veil their faces. To preach a God of comfort without awe is to preach another god altogether, and to leave men without the fear that is the beginning of wisdom.

This stripping of holy fear is no small loss, for Scripture makes the fear of the LORD the very root of knowledge and the whole duty of man. Where the fear of God is lost, wisdom is lost at its source, sin grows light, worship grows casual, and the soul flatters itself that the Holy One is indifferent to its rebellion. The recovery the age needs is not less of God’s mercy but the whole of God — holy and gracious, terrible and tender, a God to be feared and trusted at once. The Christian draws near to a God who is both consuming fire and Father; he comes with boldness through Christ, yet he comes with reverence and godly fear.
roots_summary: Hebrew yirath YHWH, the reverent awe and holy dread of God that is the beginning of wisdom.
roots_lines: The fear of the LORD — Hebrew yirath YHWH, reverent awe of God.
It is no slavish terror, yet not reverence stripped of dread.
It is the beginning of wisdom and of knowledge (Pro 9:10; 1:7).
It is the whole duty of man (Ecc 12:13).
It reaches its height in fearing Him who judges soul and body (Mat 10:28).
usage: Recover the whole God — holy and gracious, terrible and tender — against the therapeutic deity of mere comfort.
Remember that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; to lose it is to lose wisdom at its root.
Draw near to God with boldness through Christ, yet with reverence and godly fear.

etymology: The believer’s “full assurance of faith” (Heb 10:22), the settled certainty of his interest in Christ by the witness of the Spirit.
biblical_def: Assurance of faith is the settled certainty a believer may attain that he is indeed in a state of grace, accepted in Christ, and an heir of eternal life. It is no presumption, but a grace held out in Scripture and to be diligently sought. The Apostle bids us “draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith” (Heb 10:22), and witnesses that “the Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God” (Rom 8:16). John wrote his Epistle for this very end: “These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life” (1Jo 5:13). And Peter exhorts, “give diligence to make your calling and election sure” (2Pe 1:10), joining assurance to a holy and fruitful walk. The 1689 Confession teaches that this certain assurance does not so belong to the essence of faith but that a true believer may wait long and conflict with many difficulties before he obtain it; it is founded on the blood and righteousness of Christ, the inward evidence of the graces of the Spirit, and the testimony of the Spirit of adoption. It may be shaken and intermitted by negligence or by falling into sin, yet the believer is never utterly destitute of that seed of God and life of faith by which it may in due time be revived. Assurance, rightly held, fills the heart with peace, love, and holy obedience.
webster_summary: The settled certainty a believer may attain of his interest in Christ, founded on Christ’s work, the Spirit’s witness, and the fruit of grace.
webster_full: ASSURANCE OF FAITH, the believer’s settled certainty of his interest in Christ.
We may draw near in full assurance of faith (Heb 10:22).
The Spirit beareth witness that we are the children of God (Rom 8:16).
John wrote that believers may know they have eternal life (1Jo 5:13).
We are bidden to make our calling and election sure (2Pe 1:10).
scriptures: Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
Rom 8:16
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:
These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God.
Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall.
corruption_summary: Assurance is corrupted from two sides: a presumptuous easy-believism that grants false peace without fruit, and a morbid introspection that denies the believer the comfort God holds out.
corruption_paragraphs: On one side stands presumptuous easy-believism, which grants a hollow assurance on the strength of a past decision or a bare profession, while the life shows no fruit of repentance or holiness. This is a false peace, a carnal security that flatters the unconverted and forgets that Peter joins assurance to a diligent and fruitful walk: “give diligence to make your calling and election sure” (2Pe 1:10). True assurance is never severed from a holy life; the man who says he knows Christ and keeps not His commandments is a liar, and the false comfort that soothes him to sleep in his sins is among the cruelest of errors.

On the other side stands a morbid introspection, which so turns the eye inward upon the soul’s remaining corruption that it denies the believer the comfort God Himself holds out. Such a soul, ever doubting, ever digging for evidences and finding only sin, robs itself of the peace Christ purchased and dishonours the Spirit who witnesses with our spirit that we are God’s children. The 1689 Confession (ch. 18) answers both errors: assurance does not so belong to the essence of faith but that a true believer may wait long before he obtain it, yet it is a real grace, founded on Christ’s blood, the Spirit’s witness, and the inward graces, to be diligently sought and never presumed nor needlessly despaired of.
roots_summary: From the “full assurance of faith” (Heb 10:22), the believer’s certainty of his interest in Christ.
roots_lines: Assurance of faith — the believer’s certainty of his state in grace.
It is founded on the blood and righteousness of Christ.
It rests on the witness of the Spirit of adoption (Rom 8:16).
It is confirmed by the inward graces and a holy walk (2Pe 1:10).
The 1689 Confession (ch. 18) is the dictionary’s standard.
usage: Seek a true assurance founded on Christ, the Spirit’s witness, and the fruit of grace, never on a bare profession.
Reject the false peace of easy-believism that grants comfort without repentance or holiness.
Reject the morbid introspection that denies the believer the comfort God holds out in His Word.

etymology: From the Apostle’s charge to “set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth” (Col 3:2), the disposing of the soul toward heaven and Christ.
biblical_def: Heavenly-mindedness is the settled disposition of the soul that sets its affection, hope, and treasure on things above, where Christ sitteth at the right hand of God. The Apostle commands it directly: “If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God. Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth” (Col 3:1–2). It is a fixing of the inward eye upon the unseen and eternal: “we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2Co 4:18). The saints of old were marked by it, confessing themselves “strangers and pilgrims on the earth,” seeking “a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Heb 11:13–16). For the Christian’s “conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Php 3:20). Such heavenly-mindedness is no idle reverie nor flight from duty; rather it is the very spring of holy living, for the man whose treasure is above keeps his heart from the world’s snares and labours on earth as a pilgrim bound for home. The more the soul is set on Christ above, the more faithfully it walks below, loosened from covetousness, steadied under affliction, and longing for the appearing of its Lord.
webster_summary: The setting of the soul’s affection and hope on Christ and things above; the pilgrim disposition that is the spring of holy living below.
webster_full: HEAVENLY-MINDEDNESS, the setting of the soul’s affection on things above.
Set your affection on things above, not on the earth (Col 3:1–2).
Look at the things unseen and eternal, not the seen and temporal (2Co 4:18).
The saints confessed themselves strangers seeking a heavenly country (Heb 11:13–16).
Our conversation is in heaven, whence we look for the Saviour (Php 3:20).
scriptures: Col 3:1
If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.
While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
Php 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: A this-worldly prosperity-religion binds the soul to earth and treasure; and the worldly canard that one may be “too heavenly-minded” must be refused.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the this-worldly prosperity-religion that binds the soul wholly to earth — the gospel of health, wealth, and best-life-now, which makes godliness a means of earthly gain and sets the affections on the very things on earth that Paul forbids. Such a religion inverts the Apostle’s charge: instead of seeking the things above, it seeks houses, lands, and increase, dressing covetousness in the language of faith. But the Christian’s treasure is laid up in heaven, and his conversation is there; to chain the hope of the gospel to earthly prosperity is to lose the pilgrim character of the faith and to forfeit the eternal weight of glory for the perishing things that are seen.

Against the prosperity error stands also the worldly canard that one may be “too heavenly-minded to be of any earthly good” — a saying with no warrant in Scripture and flatly contrary to it. The very opposite is true: it is the most heavenly-minded saints who have done the most earthly good, for the soul whose treasure is above is loosened from covetousness, steadied under affliction, and freed to love and labour without fear. The pilgrims of Hebrews 11 who sought a better country were the very ones who subdued kingdoms and wrought righteousness. Heavenly-mindedness does not unfit a man for duty; it is the spring of it. The cure for a useless religion is not less of heaven but more.
roots_summary: From the charge to “set your affection on things above” (Col 3:2), the disposing of the soul toward heaven.
roots_lines: Heavenly-mindedness — the soul’s affection set on things above.
It seeks the things where Christ sitteth at God’s right hand (Col 3:1).
It looks at the unseen and eternal, not the seen and temporal (2Co 4:18).
It owns the pilgrim character: strangers seeking a heavenly country.
Our conversation is in heaven, whence we look for Christ (Php 3:20).
usage: Set your affection on things above; let your treasure and hope be laid up where Christ is.
Reject the prosperity-religion that binds the soul to earthly wealth and best-life-now.
Refuse the worldly canard of being “too heavenly-minded”; heavenly-mindedness is the spring of earthly good.
